concepts.name: Pitch and note names
concepts.summary: Name the seven natural notes A to G, know that pitch is how high or low a sound is, and recognise that the pattern repeats at each octave.

concepts.name: Staff, clefs and ledger lines
concepts.summary: Explain how the five-line staff and the treble and bass clefs assign pitches to lines and spaces, and how ledger lines extend the range.

concepts.name: Beat and pulse
concepts.summary: Understand the beat as the steady underlying pulse of music and tempo as its speed.

concepts.name: Note and rest values
concepts.summary: Identify whole, half, quarter and eighth notes and their matching rests, and explain how each relates in length to the others.

concepts.name: Time signatures and bars
concepts.summary: Explain what the top and bottom numbers of a simple time signature mean and how bar lines group beats into measures.

concepts.name: Sharps, flats and naturals
concepts.summary: Describe how accidentals raise or lower a pitch by a semitone and how they relate to black keys on a keyboard.

concepts.name: Semitones and whole tones
concepts.summary: Understand the semitone as the smallest step on the keyboard and the whole tone as two semitones.

concepts.name: Dynamics and basic markings
concepts.summary: Recall common dynamic markings such as p, mf and f and basic tempo terms such as allegro and andante.

misconceptions.text: Every white key is a natural note and every black key is a separate letter name unrelated to the white keys.
A faster tempo means the notes have shorter written values.
There is always a semitone between any two adjacent letter names, such as B and C or C and D.

concepts.name: Major scale construction
concepts.summary: Build a major scale on any starting note using the whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half step pattern.

concepts.name: Key signatures and the circle of fifths
concepts.summary: Identify and write the key signatures of major keys and use the circle of fifths to find how many sharps or flats a key has.

concepts.name: Scale degrees and solfège
concepts.summary: Number and name the degrees of a scale, including tonic, dominant and leading note, and relate them to solfège syllables.

concepts.name: Interval size and quality
concepts.summary: Name an interval by number and quality (major, minor, perfect) above a given note, using the major scale as reference.

concepts.name: Triads
concepts.summary: Build major and minor triads from a root by stacking thirds and distinguish them by the quality of the third.

concepts.name: Natural minor scale
concepts.summary: Construct the natural minor scale and find the relative minor of any major key.

concepts.name: Compound meter and dotted rhythms
concepts.summary: Apply dots and ties to notes and count compound time such as 6/8 in groups of three subdivisions.

concepts.name: Reading simple melodies
concepts.summary: Read a short melody in a major or minor key, naming pitches and clapping or counting its rhythm accurately.

misconceptions.text: A key signature tells you whether a piece is major or minor.
An interval's size is found by counting semitones only, so a major third and a diminished fourth are the same thing.
Minor triads sound sad and major triads sound happy because of the root note, not the third.

concepts.name: Diatonic triads and Roman numerals
concepts.summary: Build the seven triads of a major or minor key and label them with Roman numerals showing their quality and function.

concepts.name: Harmonic and melodic minor
concepts.summary: Construct harmonic and melodic minor scales and explain why the leading note is raised to create a dominant chord.

concepts.name: Chord inversions and figured bass
concepts.summary: Identify and write triads in root position and inversions and read the figures and slash chord symbols that indicate them.

concepts.name: Seventh chords
concepts.summary: Build and name the main seventh chord types, especially dominant seventh, major seventh and minor seventh.

concepts.name: Harmonic function and cadences
concepts.summary: Analyse chords as tonic, predominant or dominant function and identify authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadences.

concepts.name: Common chord progressions
concepts.summary: Analyse typical progressions such as I-IV-V-I, ii-V-I and I-vi-IV-V and explain why they feel stable or move forward.

concepts.name: Modes
concepts.summary: Construct the diatonic modes from a common scale and describe the characteristic note that distinguishes each.

concepts.name: Phrase and form structure
concepts.summary: Analyse a piece into phrases and sections such as verse, chorus, binary and ternary and describe how repetition and contrast shape it.

misconceptions.text: Minor keys use only the natural minor scale, so the V chord is always minor.
An inverted chord is a different chord with a different root.
Modes are just the major scale played starting on a different note with no difference in sound or tonal centre.

concepts.name: Secondary dominants
concepts.summary: Identify and explain chords borrowed from another key's dominant that tonicise a diatonic chord, such as V7/V.

concepts.name: Modal interchange
concepts.summary: Analyse chords borrowed from the parallel major or minor, such as iv in a major key, and judge their expressive effect.

concepts.name: Modulation techniques
concepts.summary: Analyse how a piece moves to a new key using pivot chords, common tones or direct changes and tell modulation from tonicisation.

concepts.name: Voice leading principles
concepts.summary: Evaluate chord connections by smoothness, avoiding parallel fifths and octaves and resolving tendency tones.

concepts.name: Extended and altered chords
concepts.summary: Analyse chords with added ninths, elevenths, thirteenths and alterations and explain their function within a progression.

concepts.name: Non-chord tones
concepts.summary: Distinguish passing tones, neighbour tones, suspensions and appoggiaturas and explain how they create tension against the harmony.

concepts.name: Complex and irregular rhythm
concepts.summary: Analyse syncopation, hemiola, polyrhythm and asymmetric meters such as 5/4 and 7/8 and how they affect feel.

concepts.name: Harmonic analysis of real repertoire
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing analyses of a real piece and justify a harmonic reading using evidence from the score.

misconceptions.text: Any chord with an accidental means the music has modulated to a new key.
Voice-leading rules such as banning parallel fifths are absolute laws of all music.
Non-chord tones are mistakes or notes that do not belong in the music.

concepts.name: Chromatic harmony and mediants
concepts.summary: Evaluate the use of Neapolitan, augmented sixth and chromatic mediant chords and judge how they extend tonal language.

concepts.name: Reharmonisation
concepts.summary: Create new harmonisations of a melody using substitutions and justify how each alters its character.

concepts.name: Counterpoint and texture design
concepts.summary: Compose independent melodic lines that work together and choose textures such as homophony or polyphony to suit an expressive aim.

concepts.name: Symmetrical and extended tonality
concepts.summary: Evaluate whole tone, octatonic and pentatonic systems and non-tonal approaches, judging when they replace functional harmony.

concepts.name: Arranging and orchestration
concepts.summary: Create arrangements that assign material to instruments by range, timbre and balance for a chosen ensemble.

concepts.name: Original composition in a style
concepts.summary: Compose a complete piece in a chosen idiom, integrating melody, harmony, rhythm and form with deliberate choices.

concepts.name: Critical evaluation of theory systems
concepts.summary: Evaluate the strengths and limits of analytical systems such as Roman numerals, functional theory and Schenkerian analysis for different repertoires.

misconceptions.text: Music theory is a set of rules a composer must obey to write good music.
Atonal or non-functional music has no structure or organisation.
Reharmonisation just means swapping in more complex chords, whatever the melody.
